subskill: Linear inequality from a two-plan cost context
prompt: A dance studio offers two payment plans for a season of classes. Plan A charges a $63 membership fee and a $12 shoe-rental fee, plus $6 per class. Plan B charges an $11 registration fee plus $10 per class. Plan A costs less than Plan B exactly when the number of classes n satisfies n > N, where N is a constant. What would Plan A cost, in dollars, for a member who takes exactly N classes?
explanation: Under Plan A, n classes cost 63 + 12 + 6n = 75 + 6n dollars. Under Plan B, they cost 11 + 10n dollars. Plan A costs less when 75 + 6n < 11 + 10n, which gives 64 < 4n, or n > 16. So N = 16. For 16 classes, Plan A costs 75 + 6(16) = 75 + 96 = 171 dollars. (Plan B also costs 11 + 10(16) = 171 dollars for 16 classes, which is why 16 is where Plan A starts to cost less.)
solve: const F=63+12, a=6, R=11, b=10; const N=(F-R)/(b-a); return F+a*N;

distractor_solve.99: const F=63+12, a=6, R=11, b=10; const N=(F-R)/(b+a); return F+a*N;
distractor_solve.105: const F=63+12, a=6, R=11, b=10; const N=F/(b+R-a); return F+a*N;
distractor_solve.141: const M=63, a=6, R=11, b=10; const N=(M-R)/(b-a); return M+a*N;

mechanism: write both plan costs as linear expressions
solve the strict inequality for the threshold N
evaluate Plan A's cost at N
quantity_asked: Plan A's total cost at the threshold number of classes N

plugback.why: The probe will take an option as Plan A's cost, recover n = (cost - 75)/6 using both of Plan A's fees, and check whether Plan B (11 + 10n) costs the same. All four options give a whole n under Plan A's model (4, 5, 11, 16), so the check needs Plan B's full expression too. In ascending order the key is the fourth try; 99, 105 and 141 fail first.

99.why: Moving 6n to the other side with the wrong sign gives 64 < 16n, n > 4; the slip changes a divisor, and nothing in the stem shows which way such a slip moves the cost.

105.why: Treating the $11 registration fee as a per-class charge (21 per class) puts an extra cost on Plan B; an extra charge usually raises a total, but here it sits on the comparison side and lowers the threshold to 5, so the cost falls.

141.why: Leaving out the $12 shoe-rental fee lowers the threshold (13 instead of 16) and the cost; dropping a fee from the plan with the cheaper per-class rate lowers both, but the stem gives no sign of where that lands relative to the other slips.

counter_error.solve: const F=63+12, a=6, R=11, b=10; const N=(F+R)/(b-a); return F+a*N;
counter_error.why: Moving the $11 registration fee with the wrong sign gives 86 < 4n, n > 21.5, and a Plan A cost of 204, past the key.

far_distractor.why: Counting the registration fee once per class is an over-count, which ordinarily makes a total too large; here the extra charge is on Plan B, the plan being compared against, so Plan B becomes expensive sooner, the threshold drops to 5 classes, and the resulting Plan A cost (105) lands below the key.

structure_check: No universal condition, extremum or strictest bound is asked: N is defined by an 'exactly when n > N' equivalence and the ask is a cost evaluated at N, a value both plans share. A slip on Plan A's fixed fees and a slip on Plan B's fee move the threshold in opposite directions (the registration-fee sign slip gives 204, above the key; dropping the rental gives 141, below), so the stem does not sign the errors.
intermediate_check: 141: no - Plan A's cost without the rental fee at a different threshold (13); 171 - 141 = 30 is not a printed rate or fee. 105: no - Plan A's cost at a wrong threshold of 5; 171 - 105 = 66 is not printed and no printed rate converts 105 into 171. 99: no - Plan A's cost at 4 classes; 171 - 99 = 72 is not a printed number. The one solved intermediate, N = 16, is not an option.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: Plan A costs more than its fixed fees, 75 dollars, for any positive number of classes. All four options exceed 75, so all three distractors sit on the key's side of it.
shape_check: The stem hands over: a cost in dollars (positive), above Plan A's fixed $75, and (since a member takes exactly N classes) of the form 75 + 6n with n a whole number. 99 (n = 4), 105 (n = 5), 141 (n = 11) and 171 (n = 16) all survive every property together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 105 and 141: both three-digit odd integers, same form; the key 171 is not one of them.
arith_class_check: All four are odd, all are 75 more than a multiple of 6, all exceed 75; none is a square or round number. The key is in no class alone.

subskill: Two context inequalities on one quantity; count
prompt: A gardener is filling a raised bed that already holds 6 cubic feet of soil. Each bag of soil adds 1.5 cubic feet, and the bed needs to hold at least 30 cubic feet in total. The garden store charges $4.25 per bag plus a one-time delivery fee of $15, and the gardener will spend no more than $170 in total. Only whole bags can be bought. How many different numbers of bags meet both of the gardener's requirements?
explanation: Let b be the number of bags. The soil requirement is 6 + 1.5b >= 30, so 1.5b >= 24 and b >= 16. The budget requirement is 4.25b + 15 <= 170, so 4.25b <= 155 and b <= 36.5 (to the nearest tenth). Since b is a whole number, b can be any whole number from 16 through 36. That is 36 - 16 + 1 = 21 different numbers of bags.
solve: const lo=Math.ceil((30-6)/1.5-1e-9); const hi=Math.floor((170-15)/4.25+1e-9); return hi-lo+1;

distractor_solve.17: const lo=Math.ceil(30/1.5-1e-9); const hi=Math.floor((170-15)/4.25+1e-9); return hi-lo+1;
distractor_solve.23: const lo=Math.ceil(30/1.5-6-1e-9); const hi=Math.floor((170-15)/4.25+1e-9); return hi-lo+1;
distractor_solve.28: const lo=Math.ceil((30-6)/1.5-1e-9); const hi=Math.floor((170+15)/4.25+1e-9); return hi-lo+1;

mechanism: lower bound from the volume requirement with soil already present
upper bound from the budget with a fixed fee
count whole numbers in the intersection
quantity_asked: the number of whole-number bag counts satisfying both requirements

plugback.why: The probe will try 17 first, then 21: a count cannot be substituted into either requirement; deciding whether the count is 17 or 21 means finding both bounds (16 and 36) and counting, which is the whole solution.

17.why: Ignoring the 6 cubic feet already in the bed makes the bags supply all 30 cubic feet, raising the lower bound to 20 and lowering the count; the stem does not say which way a mishandled starting amount moves a count.

23.why: Treating the 6 cubic feet as 6 bags (1.5(b + 6) >= 30) gives b >= 14 and a count of 23; the same starting amount, mishandled differently, moves the count the other way from the omission.

28.why: Moving the $15 fee with the wrong sign (4.25b <= 185) gives b <= 43 and a count of 28.

intermediate_check: 17: no - a count under a wrong lower bound (20); no printed rate or relation turns 17 into 21. 23: no - a count under a different lower bound (14); 23 is not 21 plus, minus or times any printed number. 28: no - a count under a sign-slipped upper bound; 28 - 21 = 7 is not printed. The solved intermediates (16 and 36) are not options.
shape_check: The stem hands over: a count of whole-number bag totals (positive integer); a count no larger than the number of bags the budget could ever buy (at most 36). All four options are positive integers under 36; all survive every property together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 21 and 23: both two-digit odd integers; 23 is prime and 21 = 3 x 7, neither is rounder; the key 21 is not the cleaner one.
arith_class_check: 17 odd, 21 odd, 23 odd, 28 even - the key shares its parity with two options. No multiple-of-k or roundness class singles out 21.

subskill: System of two one-variable inequalities; midpoint
prompt:
17 - 2x <= 4x - 31
4(x + 4) + 20 < 2x + 90

The numbers x that satisfy both inequalities above are exactly the numbers in an interval a <= x < b. What is the midpoint of this interval?
explanation: First inequality: 17 - 2x <= 4x - 31. Add 2x and 31 to both sides: 48 <= 6x, so x >= 8. Second inequality: 4(x + 4) + 20 < 2x + 90 gives 4x + 16 + 20 < 2x + 90, so 4x + 36 < 2x + 90, 2x < 54, and x < 27. The numbers satisfying both are 8 <= x < 27, so a = 8 and b = 27. The midpoint is (8 + 27)/2 = 35/2 = 17.5.
mechanism: solve each linear inequality for its bound
intersect the two half-lines into an interval
quantity_asked: the midpoint (a + b)/2 of the solution interval of the system

plugback.why: The probe will try 17.5 first and substitute it into both inequalities: it satisfies both, but so do 20.5, 22.5 and 25.5 (every option lies inside 8 <= x < 27), so substitution confirms nothing. Deciding which option is the midpoint needs both endpoints, 8 and 27, i.e. the whole solution.

22.5.why: Dropping the + 20 on the left of the second inequality raises its bound to 37; a dropped term usually makes an answer smaller, and nothing in the stem shows it enlarges the interval here.

20.5.why: Distributing 4 over x only (4x + 4 instead of 4x + 16) gives b = 33; the stem does not tell a student which way a distribution slip moves the midpoint.

25.5.why: Moving -2x across as -2x (so 48 <= 2x) gives a = 24; a slip on the first inequality moves the lower end, and a sign slip on its constant would move it down instead (counter_error), so the side is not readable.

counter_error.why: Moving 17 across with the wrong sign (14 <= 6x) gives a = 7/3 and a midpoint of about 14.67, below the key.

far_distractor.why: Dropping a term is an early-stop error that ordinarily lands below; here the dropped + 20 sits on the smaller side of a '<', so leaving it out loosens the upper bound from 27 to 37 and the midpoint rises to 22.5, above the key.

structure_check: No universal condition, extremum or strictest bound: the ask is the midpoint of a two-sided interval, which moves up or down with either endpoint. A slip on the lower bound can move it either way (the variable sign slip gives 25.5 above, the constant sign slip about 14.67 below), and the stem does not tell a student whether a given slip widens or narrows the interval.
intermediate_check: 22.5: no - the midpoint of a wrong interval [8, 37); no printed number turns 22.5 into 17.5 (difference 5 is not printed). 20.5: no - the midpoint of [8, 33); difference 3 is not printed. 25.5: no - the midpoint of [24, 27); 25.5 - 17.5 = 8 is the solved lower endpoint, not a printed number or rate. The solved intermediates a = 8 and b = 27 are not options.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: the second inequality alone gives x < 27, so the midpoint is under 27 (and the first gives x >= 8, so it exceeds 8). All four options lie in (8, 27), so all three distractors sit on the key's side of both bounds.
shape_check: The stem hands over: the midpoint lies inside the solution interval, so it satisfies both inequalities, and it is half of a + b. 17.5, 20.5, 22.5 and 25.5 all satisfy both inequalities and all are halves of odd integers; all four survive every property together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 20.5 and 22.5: same display form (one decimal place, .5), same complexity; the key 17.5 is not one of them.
arith_class_check: All four options end in .5; none is an integer, a multiple of 6 or a square. The key is in no class alone.

subskill: Inequality built from a linear function; value at boundary
prompt: For a certain linear function f, f(-2) = -7 and f(2) = -19. The inequality f(x - 5) >= 2f(x) - 23 holds if and only if x >= c, where c is a constant. What is the value of f(c)?
explanation: The slope of f is (-19 - (-7))/(2 - (-2)) = -12/4 = -3, so f(x) = -7 - 3(x + 2) = -3x - 13. Then f(x - 5) = -3(x - 5) - 13 = -3x + 2, and 2f(x) - 23 = 2(-3x - 13) - 23 = -6x - 49. The inequality -3x + 2 >= -6x - 49 gives 3x >= -51, so x >= -17 and c = -17. Therefore f(c) = f(-17) = -3(-17) - 13 = 51 - 13 = 38. (Check: at x = c the two sides are equal; since f(c - 5) = f(c) + 15 for this slope, f(c) + 15 = 2f(c) - 23 also gives f(c) = 38.)

distractor_solve.18: const m=(-19+7)/(2+2); const f=x=>-7+m*(x+2); const c=(2*f(0)-23-(f(0)-5))/(m-2*m); return Math.round(f(c)*1e9)/1e9;
distractor_solve.25: const m=(-19+7)/(2+2); const f=x=>-7+m*(x+2); const c=(f(0)-23-(f(0)-5*m))/(m-2*m); return Math.round(f(c)*1e9)/1e9;

mechanism: rewrite f(x - 5) and 2f(x) - 23 and solve the inequality for its boundary c
quantity_asked: f(c), the value of f at the boundary of the solution set

plugback.verify: const m=-3; const fc=v; return Math.abs((fc-5*m)-(2*fc-23))<1e-9;
plugback.why: The probe can take an option as f(c), note that f(c - 5) = f(c) + 15 once the slope -3 is known, and check whether f(c) + 15 = 2f(c) - 23. That needs the slope from the two given values and the shift relation; in ascending order the key is the fourth try, after 18, 25 and 35 fail.

18.why: Treating f(x - 5) as f(x) - 5 (shifting the output instead of the input) gives 3x >= -31 and f(c) = 18; the stem does not show whether an input/output swap raises or lowers the answer.

25.why: Reading 2f(x) as f(2x) gives -3x + 2 >= -6x - 36, c = -38/3 and f(c) = 25.

35.why: Counting the run from -2 to 2 as 5 (both endpoints) gives slope -12/5 = -2.4; the over-count goes into the divisor, so the slope's size and then f(c) shrink.

The errors do not share a side by structure: doubling the constant (counter_error) gives 61 above, the slip on the input shift gives 18 below, and a slope sign slip (+3) would change which way the inequality points, so the stem does not sign the errors.

subskill: Line meeting the region of a system of inequalities
prompt:
y >= (1/2)x - 2
y <= -2x + 13
x >= 0

In the xy-plane, the solutions to the system of inequalities above form a triangular region. The line y = -4x + c, where c is a constant, contains at least one point of this region exactly when p <= c <= q. What is the value of q - p?
explanation: The region is a triangle. Two corners are on the y-axis: (0, -2) and (0, 13). The third corner is where the two slanted boundary lines meet: (1/2)x - 2 = -2x + 13 gives (5/2)x = 15, so x = 6 and y = (1/2)(6) - 2 = 1, giving (6, 1). For a line y = -4x + c, c = y + 4x. As the parallel lines y = -4x + c slide across the triangle, the value of c first and last touches the region at corners, so p and q are the least and greatest values of y + 4x at the three corners: (0, -2) gives -2, (0, 13) gives 13, and (6, 1) gives 1 + 24 = 25. So p = -2 and q = 25, and q - p = 25 - (-2) = 27.
solve: const X=(2+13)/(0.5+2), Y=0.5*X-2; const v=[-2,13,Y+4*X]; return Math.max(...v)-Math.min(...v);

distractor_solve.36: const X=(2+13)/(0.5+2), Y=0.5*X-2; const v=[-2,13,Y-4*X]; return Math.max(...v)-Math.min(...v);
distractor_solve.60: const X=(2+13)/(0.5-2), Y=0.5*X-2; const v=[-2,13,Y+4*X]; return Math.max(...v)-Math.min(...v);

evaluate at the corners and take the range
quantity_asked: q - p, the length of the interval of c for which the line meets the region
